what_it_does: Inside a computer chip, a 'clock tree' is the network of wires that distributes a timing signal to every part of the chip so that all the transistors act in unison. If some parts receive the clock signal slightly earlier than others (called 'clock skew'), the chip may malfunction or have to run more slowly. Clock tree designers must also minimize the total wire length to save cost and power. These two goals — low skew and low wire length — conflict with each other, and choosing the right intermediate relay points (called hub nodes) in the tree is the key decision. This paper uses reinforcement learning (an AI technique where an agent learns by trial and reward, like training a dog with treats) to automatically find hub node placements that balance this tradeoff better than manual or simpler automated methods.
